structured_output.summary: Twelve outside results. (1) Settles H1.5.4 by reading code: the reference airbench94_muon rescales every conv filter to norm sqrt(out_channels) after each step (p.data.mul_(len(p.data)**0.5 / p.data.norm())). If the port kept that line, weight decay on the filters has no effect: E016's gain came from the SGD groups, and Muon weight decay is a free parameter. The reference also uses 3 Newton-Schulz steps with coefficients (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315), which is relevant to H1.2.3. (2) Lowers the prior for H6.4 and H6.4.2: NVIDIA's guidance says channel counts divisible by 8 are enough for fp16 tensor cores, so Cin=24 already qualifies. Efficient tiling wants 64–256, and padding 24→32 reaches neither. E043 also attributes half of the freeze's saving to memory-bound kernels. (3) The Hiverge record (CIFAR-10) differs from the port in several untested ways: SiLU in the conv groups, BN eps 1e-12 and momentum 0.5566 with frozen BN weights, LS 0.09, batch 1536 with 7.65 epochs, tuned Newton-Schulz coefficients (3.4576, -4.7391, 2.0843), filter renormalization that gets less frequent over training (every 4 steps rising to 2+15·progress), brightness/contrast jitter of 0.14/0.13, and no warm-up. (4) The Fable/Fulcrum CIFAR-10 write-up: the 24→28→32 px curriculum gave −0.209 s of about 2.0 s, and the systems work (CUDA-graphing the whole run, fused optimizer) gave nothing measurable. That matches E015/E017, so H2.2 is exhausted. (5) The airbench paper: alternating flip's gain is largest without TTA (about 27% effective speedup at 20 epochs), which supports keeping it (H1.4). (6) A100 PCIe vs SXM4: 300 W vs 400 W, 1935 vs 2039 GB/s (about 5% less bandwidth), the same 312 TFLOP/s dense fp16 peak. One source says single-GPU performance is largely similar; a second claims NVIDIA quotes about 10% lower sustained performance (search snippet only, not verified). This bears on H4.3: expect the judge's absolute time to be higher, but the ranking of levers should mostly hold. (7) Muon critical-batch paper: the critical batch shrinks as momentum rises, Nesterov shifts it larger, and Muon was most efficient at every batch size tested on CIFAR. This is weak, indirect evidence for H5. (8) Turbo-Muon removes one Newton-Schulz iteration; with Newton-Schulz at about 2.5% of the step (E043), that is at most about 1% of time. (9) Ghost BN is reported to help most at batch sizes in the thousands and costs about 5% throughput. It is an untested accuracy booster at batch 2000 (new direction; low to moderate prior given E016's evidence of over-regularization). (10) Lavin: memory-bound BN and activation layers are a large share of convnet time, and only block-level fusion removes them. Inductor cannot fold training-mode BN into conv epilogues, so the 27% fused-kernel share (E043) can only shrink through fewer BN layers or activations, or custom kernels. (11) A critical-damping momentum schedule loses 1.7 pp on CIFAR-100: negative evidence for momentum-schedule tricks. (12) An auto-research paper's 4.6% speedup on CIFAR-10 airbench96 came only from a shorter schedule, a higher LR and a faster warm-up. Nothing new.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon rescales every conv filter after each optimizer step: p.data.mul_(len(p.data)**0.5 / p.data.norm()). Weight decay is wd = 2e-6*batch_size, divided by each group's lr. Newton-Schulz runs steps=3 with a,b,c = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315). Muon lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov. SGD momentum 0.85, bias_lr 0.053, head_lr 0.67. Batch 2000, 8 epochs, LS 0.2, BN momentum 0.6, eps 1e-12, GELU, widths 64/256/256. Whitening bias trained for 3 epochs' worth of steps. Evaluation uses TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: Settles H1.5.4 by reading code: if the port copies the per-step renormalization, decay on the Muon filters is undone every step, so E016's gain came from the SGD groups (BN biases at 64x lr, whitening bias, head) and changing filter wd does nothing. Also gives the reference Newton-Schulz count (3) to compare with the port for H1.2.3. The CIFAR-10 recipe reached 94% only with TTA level 2, which is banned here.

findings.claim: NVIDIA: 'Choose the number of input and output channels to be divisible by 8 (for FP16) ... to run efficiently on Tensor Cores'. For efficient tiling, choose batch and channels 'divisible by at least 64 and ideally 256'. Use NHWC (channels_last). Specialized kernels exist for C=4 in first layers.
findings.relevance: Cin=24 already satisfies the fp16 tensor-core rule (a multiple of 8), so the claim that group-1 conv1 runs at low tensor-core efficiency because of misalignment is weaker than H6.4 assumes. Padding to 32 (H6.4.2) does not reach the 64/256 tiling sweet spot either. Expect a gain under 2%; if alignment is tested at all, padding to 64 is the meaningful version, though it adds MACs. E043 shows about half the freeze's saving was memory-bound fused kernels, which points to H6.3 over H6.4.

findings.claim: Hiverge's CIFAR-10 record: SiLU in the conv groups (GELU only before the first group). BN momentum 0.5566 (stored as 0.4434), eps 1e-12, BN weight frozen (requires_grad False), bias trainable. Whitening 2x2, 24 channels, initialized by SVD, bias trained for ceil(0.2*steps per epoch). Widths 64/256/256. Batch 1536, 7.65 epochs. Muon lr 0.205, momentum 0.655. SGD momentum 0.825, bias lr 0.0573, head lr 0.5415. wd = 1.0418e-6*batch (~0.0016). LS 0.09. Newton-Schulz: 3 steps with a,b,c = (3.4576, -4.7391, 2.0843). Filter renormalization every 4 steps, rising to every 2+int(15*progress). Brightness jitter 0.1399, contrast 0.1308. Selective TTA. compile mode max-autotune, fullgraph. fp16 data and momentum buffers. Linear LR decay to 0 with no warm-up.
findings.relevance: Gives the untested deltas between this port and the record: Newton-Schulz coefficients and renormalization frequency (H1.2.3), LS 0.09 (H1.5.5), brightness/contrast jitter (H1.5.8), batch 1536 under Muon (H5.1.2), and SiLU. One caveat on H2.6.3: the whitening bias trains for 20% of one epoch's steps, not 20% of all steps. Hiverge stops it after about 20 steps, so E036's detach at 20% of the run (about 46 steps) could move earlier.

findings.claim: Fable's best CIFAR-10 run (94% in 1.828 s vs Hiverge's 1.978 s): the 24→28→32 px curriculum saved −0.209 s in total (−0.128 s from adding 28→32, −0.081 s from deepening to 24 px). A 24 px step costs 0.56x a 32 px step. MaxPool2d(3) was replaced by a true global max pool (x.flatten(2).max(2)), at negligible cost at 32 px (2.298 vs 2.283 s). The systems work (CUDA graph over the whole ~284-step run, foreach-fused optimizer, compile hygiene) contributed nothing measurable (about 0.04 s, within noise). The detailed analysis is in investigations/24px-curriculum.md.
findings.relevance: Outside replication of E007/E015/E017: progressive resizing is about a 10% lever on airbench-style nets, and launch overhead and optimizer fusion are exhausted once the step is GPU-bound. That supports retiring further H2.2 work. The 0.56x cost of a 24 px step vs the 0.5625 pixel ratio confirms pixel-proportional scaling for tile-friendly sizes (H6.2).

findings.claim: airbench paper: patch-whitening initialization is the single most impactful feature (45→21 epochs). Alternating flip gives a 15–102% effective speedup, largest without TTA (about 27% at 20 epochs). Lookahead cut the A100 time from 5.1 to 4.6 s. BN affine scale is disabled, BN momentum 0.6, LS 0.2. airbench96 reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100 vs ResNet-18's 77.54% (no Cutout).
findings.relevance: Supports H1.4: with TTA banned, alternating flip is worth more and must be kept. The Lookahead gain in the paper (~10%) is consistent with E005's +0.97 pp on CIFAR-100. No GELU-vs-ReLU ablation exists, so the activation choice is untested in the lineage.

findings.claim: A100 80GB PCIe: 300 W TDP, 1,935 GB/s. SXM4: 400 W, 2,039 GB/s (about 5% more bandwidth). Dense FP16 tensor peak is the same, 312 TFLOP/s. Hyperstack says 'single-GPU performance is largely similar between PCIe and SXM'. A search snippet (not verified on a fetched page) says NVIDIA quotes about 10% lower performance for PCIe in sustained workloads, because the power cap limits clocks.
findings.relevance: Bears on H4.3: bandwidth-bound levers (the stem freeze and whitening detach, about half memory-bound per E043) lose about 5% of their absolute saving on the judge. Compute-bound levers (resolution, epochs) may be hit more by power-cap throttling. Absolute judged time should come in roughly 5–10% above local, but the lever ranking should hold. The 8.11 s PCIe result of the abdullah-athar fork vs this loop's 5.31 s on SXM4 cannot be compared directly.

findings.claim: Muon convergence and critical-batch paper: experiments on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, VGG-16/CIFAR-100 and Llama-160M/C4. Muon was the most efficient optimizer at every batch size tested on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10. Nesterov shifts the critical batch to larger values. The critical batch decreases as momentum β rises (Fig. 4). Weight decay slightly raises it. Theory requires lr·wd ≤ 1.
findings.relevance: Weak, indirect evidence for H5: with Nesterov and a low Muon momentum (0.6), the critical batch should be on the larger side, which slightly favours H5.1.1/H5.1.3 (batch can grow without penalty) over H5.1.2 (smaller batch buys accuracy). It does not settle the short-run, under-fitting regime (E045 leaned toward steps carrying accuracy).

findings.claim: Turbo-Muon: almost-orthogonal preconditioning speeds up Newton-Schulz convergence, so one of the usual five iterations can be removed without losing approximation quality. Up to 2.8x faster Newton-Schulz and 5–10% end-to-end on efficiency tasks, with no tuning.
findings.relevance: Limits the value of H1.2.3. E043 measured Newton-Schulz plus the head GEMMs at about 0.8 ms of a 33.5 ms step (about 2.5%). If the port uses 5 steps, cutting to 3 (reference) could save about 1%. If it already uses 3, the remaining Newton-Schulz lever is under 1%, below H1.2.3's 1.5% threshold.

findings.claim: Ghost BatchNorm computes BN statistics over smaller 'ghost' sub-batches. It acts as a regularizer that makes large-batch training behave like small-batch training. The original paper reports 0–3% accuracy changes, with some evidence it helps more at batch sizes in the thousands. Composer measured about 5% lower throughput on ResNet-50/ImageNet.
findings.relevance: New, untested direction (a candidate H1.5 or H5 child): at batch 2000, ghost BN (e.g. 4×500 via a reshape inside the compiled graph) could add accuracy at near-zero step count. Cost: extra reduction kernels in an already 27% memory-bound fused share (E043), plus some time. The prior is low to moderate, because E016/E022 suggest this recipe is over-regularized rather than under-regularized. It also offers a way to test H5 (steps vs batch-noise effects) without changing the step count.

findings.claim: Lavin, 'On the Efficiency of Convolutional Neural Networks': memory-bound layers (BN, activations, degenerate convs) have low computational efficiency and dominate latency more than FLOPs suggest. Block-fusion kernels that run a whole residual block in one kernel restore temporal locality and gave about 4x over ConvNeXt for the ConvFirst model.
findings.relevance: Outside support for H6.3: the 27% memory-bound fused BN/GELU/pointwise share in E043 is a known pattern, and only fusion across the conv boundary (or removing BN/activation layers) cuts it. Training-mode BN needs a full reduction over the conv output, so Inductor cannot fold it into a conv epilogue. Realistic lever candidates: fewer BN layers per group, or a conv+BN-stats epilogue as a custom Triton kernel (high effort).

findings.claim: Critical-damping momentum schedule μ(t)=1−2√α(t): 2.34x faster to 90% on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 but −0.46 pp final accuracy. On CIFAR-100 the speedup shrinks to 1.14x and the accuracy cost grows to −1.7 pp. Layer selection by gradient attribution was no better than random.
findings.relevance: Negative evidence for momentum or LR schedule-shape tricks on CIFAR-100 short runs, consistent with E009/E029 (the schedule shape is flat). Argues against spending runs on optimizer-schedule reshaping (H1.6).

findings.claim: Multi-agent auto-research on CIFAR-10 airbench96 (0.96 gate): 26.356 s → 25.146 s (−4.59%). Every gain came from skipping logging-only validation calls, shortening the schedule, raising LR intensity, and a faster warm-up that repaired the accuracy margin after a near-miss.
findings.relevance: The outside agent loop found no new mechanisms beyond the schedule and LR dials, consistent with H4.2 (epochs as the main dial) and with near-miss repair through warm-up. E029 found warm-up flat on this recipe, so expect little from that route here.
